newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to aid Hanbo to limit impact on economy.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to aid Hanbo to limit impact on economy.

text.p: South Korea plans to set aside about 100 billion won ($115 million) to keep struggling Hanbo Steel Co running and to help the company's suppliers weather Hanbo's problems, Finance Ministry officials said on Friday.

Finance and Economy Minister Han Seung-soo, in a meeting between President Kim Young-sam and his top economic officials, said the emergency fund would help Hanbo pay for raw materials and transportation expenses, the ministry officials said.
It would also be used to pay wages of workers at Hanbo's suppliers and subcontractors.
The move came as state prosecutors grilled founder Chung Tae-soo of the Hanbo Group over a loan scandal surrounding the group's steelmaking unit.

Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's 14th-largest conglomerate, defaulted on debt repayments last week after piling up about five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans from 61 banks and financial institutions.
During Friday's meeting, Kim ordered that something be done to allow Hanbo Steel to keep operating, a statement from the presidential Blue House said.
Kim said Hanbo Group's problems, which followed nearly a month of nationwide labour strife, posed further difficulties to the already slowing economy.

"Steps should be taken to aid smooth production at Hanbo Steel plants which are already operational," Kim said. "A fair assessment must be made of the mill under construction and it should be completed as scheduled if it proves to be feasible."

Hanbo Steel and three affiliates are awaiting court rulings on their applications for receivership. A Seoul court said on Friday it had decided to freeze Hanbo Steel assets until a decision was made on the receivership.
Kim, who ordered a thorough probe into the loans on Monday, said the crisis appeared to stem from Hanbo Steel's heavy reliance on borrowing to fund excessive expansion.
He said although the government could not unfairly support one company, it was necessary to stop the steelmaker's failure from harming the economy.
State prosecutors said they were questioning Chung and officials from Hanbo and its creditor banks on how billions of dollars were funnelled to the financially shaky Hanbo Steel.

Chung was summoned from a hospital on Thursday and questioned overnight. Chung had been admitted to hospital after complaining of high blood pressure on Tuesday but doctors said his health was relatively sound.
Prosecutors said they suspected Chung was involved in "illegal activities". No details were given.
Chung acquired or set up 18 companies in the past three years to make the Hanbo Group South Korea's 14th-largest conglomerate, or chaebol, with 22 units.

Opposition parties, calling the loans the biggest financial scandal in the country's history, have accused the government of pressuring creditor banks to offer loans to Hanbo without adequate collateral.

Kim came to power in 1993 on an anti-graft platform and gave top priority to severing the corrupt alliance betweeen politics and business, which he described as the worst legacy of the military-backed rule of his predecessors.
